title: Investor Renovation Contractor in Baltimore, MD | Genstone
metaDescription: Baltimore rowhouse rehabs for investors and lenders: flips, BRRRR, rentals, conversions, 203(k) and REO, scoped for VBNs, rental licenses and Maryland lead law.
intro: Baltimore rewards investors who can read a rowhouse. Under the formstone front in Highlandtown, behind the marble steps in Pigtown, past the porch of a daylight row in Belair-Edison, the same questions decide your margin: how sound the party walls and rear wall are, what the flat roof is hiding, whether the house carries a Vacant Building Notice, and what it will take to pass Maryland's lead rules and Baltimore's rental licensing. Genstone Construction renovates Baltimore properties for individual investors, lenders, servicers and funds by coordinating vetted, licensed local contractors, with a designated field manager on each project and oversight from our Romeoville, Illinois headquarters. Our free Pre-Offer Rehab Review estimates repairs and checks the after-repair value against the specific block before you commit. After you buy, you get a written scope with labor, materials and draws, permits through the Department of Housing and Community Development, lien waivers collected and progress you can follow from anywhere.
housingStock:
Baltimore is one of the great rowhouse cities, and its rows span nearly two centuries. The oldest investor-grade houses are the small two- and two-and-a-half-story brick alley houses and workers' rows of Fells Point, Washington Hill and parts of South Baltimore, many with dormers, shallow footprints and stairs tucked against the party wall. Through the middle of the nineteenth century, the city added tall Italianate rows with high ceilings, ornate cornices and long rear wings in Union Square, Bolton Hill, Mount Vernon and Reservoir Hill, many later divided into apartments.

The late 1800s and early 1900s brought the familiar two- and three-story brick rows of Highlandtown, Canton, Pigtown, Patterson Park and Charles Village, often with marble steps and, after the 1940s and 1950s, a coat of formstone over the original brick. Hampden and Woodberry mix stone and brick mill workers' houses along the Jones Falls. From the 1910s into the 1940s, builders put up daylight rowhouses, wider two-story rows designed so every room has a window, with front porches in Belair-Edison, Ednor Gardens-Lakeside, Waverly, Rosemont and Edmondson Village. Hamilton and Lauraville add bungalows, foursquares and detached shingle houses.

For a rehab, most of this stock shares masonry party walls, flat or low-slope roofs drained to the rear, brick or stone foundations, plaster interiors, pre-1978 lead paint and basements with limited headroom. Rear additions and back buildings were often built later and with less care, so they are frequent sources of settlement and roof leaks. Formstone can hide deteriorated brick, failed lintels and water damage. Many houses still carry ungrounded wiring, galvanized supply lines, cast-iron stacks and older sewer laterals, and the city has been working on lead service line issues in older neighborhoods.

commonIssues.title: Vacant Building Notices
commonIssues.body: Baltimore issues Vacant Building Notices on properties it considers vacant and unfit, and thousands of houses carry them. A VBN generally means the property cannot be legally occupied until the violations are corrected under permit and the city clears the notice. That affects financing, insurance and timeline. We check VBN status during the Pre-Offer Rehab Review and scope the work needed to abate it, including any structural repairs, so the property can be inspected, cleared and occupied.

commonIssues.title: Rear walls, back buildings and roofs
commonIssues.body: Many Baltimore rows have a rear addition or back building with a lighter foundation and its own roof. Over time, these sections settle away from the main house, crack at the junction and leak where the roofs meet. Flat roofs throughout the city often have multiple layers of coating over failing membranes. We assess the rear wall, back building foundation and roof system together, and we price repairs that address the cause rather than recoating over a problem that will reappear.

commonIssues.title: Formstone and what it hides
commonIssues.body: Formstone, the cement-based stone imitation applied to thousands of Baltimore facades in the mid-twentieth century, can trap moisture and hide cracked brick, rusted lintels and failing mortar. Some buyers love it; others want it removed to reveal original brick. Removal can be costly and may expose damage that needs repair. We assess the facade carefully and price options so the decision fits your strategy and the neighborhood's buyer expectations.

commonIssues.title: Maryland lead rules for rentals
commonIssues.body: Maryland's lead law requires owners of rental housing built before 1978 to register units with the Maryland Department of the Environment and obtain lead risk reduction certificates at turnover. Baltimore's rental licensing also depends on lead compliance. That makes lead-safe work practices, window treatment and specialized cleaning essential parts of any rental rehab. We plan scopes so the unit is ready for the required inspection and dust testing when construction ends.

commonIssues.title: Sewer backups and older plumbing
commonIssues.body: Older Baltimore rows commonly have cast-iron stacks, galvanized supply lines and clay or cast-iron laterals. Heavy rain has caused sewage backups into basements in parts of the city, and basement floor drains are often the entry point. We recommend camera inspection of the lateral on most purchases and often include lateral repair, cleanouts and backwater valves. Replacing supply lines and checking the service line material during the rehab also reduces future leaks and tenant complaints.

investorMarket:
Baltimore's investor market varies dramatically from one neighborhood to the next, and sometimes within a single block. Flips tend to perform best where buyers already pay for renovated rows: Canton, Patterson Park, Highlandtown, Brewers Hill, Federal Hill, Hampden, Remington and parts of Charles Village. Buyers in those areas often include hospital and university employees, young professionals and newcomers from Washington and elsewhere who expect finished basements, renovated kitchens and baths, central air and roof decks on some blocks.

The northeast neighborhoods, including Hamilton, Lauraville, Belair-Edison and Ednor Gardens-Lakeside, are popular with owner-occupants and long-term landlords. Their daylight rows and detached homes offer more space and porches at prices below the waterfront neighborhoods, making them strong areas for BRRRR, single-family rentals and 203(k) purchases.

In West and Southwest Baltimore, including Edmondson Village, Morrell Park, Pigtown and parts of Sandtown-Winchester and Harlem Park, purchase prices can be low but scopes are often heavy. Many houses carry Vacant Building Notices, and deals there depend on accurate structural assessment, realistic rents and a clear path through permitting and licensing.

Small multifamily is concentrated in Reservoir Hill, Bolton Hill, Charles Village and Mount Vernon, where large Victorian rows were divided into apartments, though the legal unit count must be confirmed. Bank-owned and servicer inventory appears throughout the city and in older inner suburbs like Dundalk and Essex. Our Pre-Offer Rehab Review prices the specific property and block, because averages are misleading in Baltimore.
permits:
Building, electrical, plumbing and mechanical permits in Baltimore are issued through the Department of Housing and Community Development, which also handles inspections, code enforcement and Vacant Building Notices. Structural repairs, rear wall rebuilding, new openings, roof decks, additions and system replacements generally require permits and inspections, and work to abate a VBN must be permitted before the city will clear it. Home improvement contractors in Maryland must hold a license from the Maryland Home Improvement Commission, and electrical and plumbing work must be performed by appropriately licensed trades.

Converting a rowhouse into apartments or changing its use generally requires zoning approval, and many conversions require a hearing before the Board of Municipal and Zoning Appeals. Properties in local historic districts, such as Bolton Hill, Mount Vernon, Union Square and Butchers Hill, need approval from the Commission for Historical and Architectural Preservation, known as CHAP, for exterior changes.

Rental properties in Baltimore must be registered and licensed with the city, and licensing requires an inspection by a Maryland-licensed home inspector along with lead compliance for pre-1978 units through the Maryland Department of the Environment. Your Genstone field manager tracks permits, VBN status, inspections and licensing documentation for each property so the house is ready to occupy when the work is done.
climate: Baltimore has hot, humid summers, cold but variable winters and plenty of freeze-thaw cycles in between. Humidity drives basement moisture, mold and condensation in rows without adequate ventilation or air conditioning. Freeze-thaw damage shows up in mortar joints, marble and concrete steps and the junction between back buildings and main houses. Flat roofs take a beating from summer heat and winter ice, which is why roof membranes and flashing at party walls fail often. Heavy rainstorms and the remnants of tropical systems can overwhelm older drainage and push water into basements, and low areas near the harbor and the Jones Falls are vulnerable to flooding. For scheduling, roofing, masonry, formstone removal and exterior painting are best from spring through fall. Interior work continues through winter once the house is closed in and heated, though vacant houses need careful winterization to prevent frozen pipes.

faqs.q: Do you work in Baltimore County as well as the city?
faqs.a: Yes. We coordinate vetted, licensed local contractors in Baltimore City and in nearby Baltimore County and Anne Arundel County communities such as Towson, Dundalk, Catonsville, Essex, Parkville and Glen Burnie. Permits outside the city are handled by the relevant county, and your field manager files with the right office. Genstone manages projects from our Romeoville, Illinois headquarters, with a designated field manager assigned to every job.

faqs.q: Can you renovate a house with a Vacant Building Notice?
faqs.a: Yes. Many Baltimore investment properties carry VBNs. We review the notice and the property's condition, scope the work needed to correct the violations and pull the required permits through the Department of Housing and Community Development. Once the work passes inspection, the notice can be cleared and the house occupied. We include VBN status in our Pre-Offer Rehab Review so it is factored into your price and schedule.

faqs.q: What do I owe before construction starts?
faqs.a: Nothing. Genstone asks for no upfront payment on Baltimore projects. Draws are released as stages of work are completed and documented by your field manager with photos and milestone updates, and final payment comes after completion and your approval. Dumpster and debris costs are included in the estimate, which matters on narrow Baltimore streets where demolition debris often leaves through the front door and dumpster placement may need a permit.

faqs.q: Does Genstone warranty its Baltimore work?
faqs.a: Yes. We provide a one-year workmanship warranty on the work we perform, covering problems such as a roof membrane seam that was not properly sealed or a fixture installed incorrectly. It excludes damage caused by occupants and the ordinary wear a rowhouse sees over time. If a covered issue arises, your field manager coordinates the repair and uses the project documentation to confirm what was installed and when.

fix-flip.title: Fix and Flip Contractor in Baltimore, MD | Genstone
fix-flip.metaDescription: Baltimore flip renovations for Canton, Hampden and Hamilton rowhouses: block-level comps, rear walls, roof decks, formstone decisions and milestone-based draws.
fix-flip.h1: Fix and Flip Renovations in Baltimore
fix-flip.intro: Baltimore flip buyers are specific about what they want, and it depends on the neighborhood. In Canton and Patterson Park, they expect a finished basement, an open first floor, two full baths and sometimes a roof deck with a harbor view. In Hamilton or Lauraville, they want a porch, a yard and a house that feels solid. In Hampden, they may care more about character than square footage. Genstone Construction helps you plan flips that fit the block, not an average. Our free Pre-Offer Rehab Review estimates repairs and checks the after-repair value against recent sales nearby, and flags Baltimore-specific risks like Vacant Building Notices, failing back buildings and formstone damage. Once you own the house, a designated field manager coordinates vetted local contractors, permits through Housing and Community Development, and draws tied to completed work.

sections.h2: Setting the finish level street by street
sections.body:
Flip values in Baltimore are hyperlocal. A renovated row in Canton or Brewers Hill may be competing with other high-end rehabs and new construction, while a similar row a short walk away in Highlandtown or Patterson Park East might sell to buyers who prioritize price over a roof deck. Comps from even a few blocks away can mislead.

Our estimators build multiple ARV plans for each property. One plan might focus on systems, a kitchen and baths, and a clean basement. Another might add a second or third bath, finish the basement with proper waterproofing, open the first floor and add a roof deck where structure and zoning allow. Each plan includes its own scope, cost and projected value. For daylight rows in the northeast, a front porch rebuild, updated kitchen and a finished lower level can make the strongest impression, while in Hampden, restored original details can matter as much as new finishes. You choose the plan the block supports instead of guessing.

In most Baltimore rows, joists run from party wall to party wall, so many interior walls are non-bearing and open first floors are achievable. The real costs tend to be elsewhere. Rear walls and back buildings often need foundation repair, rebuilding or tie-ins where they have separated from the main house. Flat roofs are usually replaced on a flip, with careful flashing at both party walls and at the back building junction.

Basements are the other major decision. Buyers like finished lower levels, but many Baltimore basements have low ceilings, stone walls and sewer lines running beneath the floor. Finishing one properly requires waterproofing, drainage, a sump where needed, a backwater valve and sometimes underpinning or lowering the floor to gain headroom. Formstone is another choice: removing it can reveal attractive brick but may expose damage and add cost. We price each of these decisions separately, so you can see how they affect your margin before committing.

Every month a Baltimore flip sits unfinished costs interest, insurance, taxes and utilities. If the property carries a Vacant Building Notice, it also cannot be occupied until the notice is cleared, which makes permitting central to your timeline. We prepare permit applications early, often before closing when access is available, and identify any structural or zoning reviews needed for roof decks, additions or back building rebuilds.

Once permits are in hand, the field manager sequences demolition, structural and masonry repairs, rough plumbing, electrical and HVAC, inspections, insulation and drywall, then finishes. Exterior masonry, roofing and formstone work are scheduled for favorable weather when possible, while interior work continues regardless. Dumpster placement on narrow streets may require a permit, and that cost is included in our estimate. Draws are released only for completed work, and at the end you receive permit records, inspection results, VBN clearance where applicable and lien waivers, which buyers' agents and title companies frequently request.

faqs.q: Should I add a roof deck to a Baltimore flip?
faqs.a: It depends on the block. In Canton, Federal Hill, Brewers Hill and parts of Patterson Park, roof decks are common in renovated homes and can help a flip compete. In other neighborhoods, buyers may not pay for one. Roof decks require permits, structural framing and careful roofing, and may need zoning review. Our Pre-Offer Rehab Review can price your flip with and without a deck so you can compare the projected return.

faqs.q: Should I remove formstone from a Baltimore row?
faqs.a: Sometimes. Removing formstone can reveal original brick that buyers like, but it can also expose cracked brick, failed lintels or water damage that requires repair. Some buyers appreciate formstone as part of Baltimore's character. We assess the facade, estimate the cost of removal and repair, and compare it with nearby sales so you can decide whether it adds value on your block.

faqs.q: Can you flip a property with a Vacant Building Notice?
faqs.a: Yes. Many flips start as VBN properties. The work required to correct the violations must be permitted, and the city must clear the notice before the house can be occupied or sold to an owner-occupant. We include VBN abatement in the scope and schedule, and your field manager coordinates the inspections needed to clear it as the renovation progresses toward listing.

brrrr.title: BRRRR Contractor in Baltimore, MD | Genstone
brrrr.metaDescription: Baltimore BRRRR rehabs built for the refi appraisal, city rental licensing and Maryland lead certificates: durable daylight-row scopes and documented draws.
brrrr.intro: Baltimore's daylight rows and porch-front homes in Belair-Edison, Ednor Gardens-Lakeside, Hamilton and Edmondson Village are a common starting point for BRRRR investors. Purchase prices leave room for a full renovation, and steady tenant demand supports long-term holds. The catch is that a Baltimore rental must clear more hurdles than in many cities: a refinance appraisal, Maryland's lead risk reduction requirements, the city's rental license inspection and, often, a Vacant Building Notice. Genstone Construction scopes rehabs to clear all of them. Our free Pre-Offer Rehab Review estimates repairs and refines the after-repair value before you buy. After closing, a designated field manager coordinates vetted local contractors, permits through Housing and Community Development and the documentation your lender, appraiser and licensing inspector will need. Draws are tied to completed work, and the last payment follows your approval.

sections.body:
Appraisers valuing a renovated Baltimore row look for recent sales of similar homes in similar condition, usually within the same neighborhood. Because values can shift from block to block, the immediate comps matter most. In northeast neighborhoods with many renovated daylight rows, a thorough rehab can produce a predictable appraisal. In areas with few renovated sales, appraisals may lag even after quality work.

We review likely comparables before recommending a scope. Items that appear clearly on an appraisal report tend to carry the most weight: a new roof, updated electrical service, new HVAC with central air, renovated kitchen and baths, replacement windows and a dry, usable basement. Adding a second full bath can matter in rows that originally had one. A finished basement may add value where comparables have them, but only if it is properly waterproofed. We document every improvement with photos and an itemized list so the appraiser can see the full scope, especially when the property started with a VBN or severe deterioration.

Before a Baltimore rental can be leased, it must be registered and licensed with the city, which requires an inspection by a Maryland-licensed home inspector. Pre-1978 rentals must also comply with Maryland's lead law, including registration with the Maryland Department of the Environment and a lead risk reduction certificate based on inspection and dust testing.

Lead and licensing therefore get written into a Baltimore BRRRR scope on day one. Lead compliance often means replacing original windows or treating friction and impact surfaces, stabilizing deteriorated paint inside and out, covering or treating bare soil where required and performing specialized cleaning before dust-wipe testing. Licensing inspections focus on smoke and carbon monoxide alarms, safe egress, handrails, heat, electrical safety and plumbing. If you plan to accept vouchers through the Housing Authority of Baltimore City, the unit will also face that program's inspection. Building all of this into the rehab means the house is ready for a tenant as soon as the refinance closes.

A BRRRR property needs to hold up for years of tenants. In Baltimore rows, original hardwood floors can often be refinished, but where floors are damaged or uneven, luxury vinyl plank is durable and affordable to replace. Kitchens and baths benefit from standard cabinet lines, solid-surface or laminate counters and tile or vinyl that handles water. Washable paint simplifies turns.

Systems are where long-term costs live. Flat roofs should be replaced properly with good flashing rather than recoated. Older boilers and radiators may be kept and serviced, while many investors choose new forced-air systems with central air because tenants and appraisers expect cooling. Electrical panels should be updated, and galvanized supply lines replaced. Sewer laterals deserve a camera inspection, with lining or replacement as needed and a backwater valve where appropriate. Porches on daylight rows need sound framing and railings. Addressing these items during the rehab reduces emergencies and protects your cash flow after the refinance.

faqs.q: Which Baltimore neighborhoods suit a BRRRR strategy?
faqs.a: Investors often focus on northeast neighborhoods such as Belair-Edison, Ednor Gardens-Lakeside, Hamilton and Lauraville, along with Edmondson Village and parts of Southwest Baltimore. These areas offer daylight rows and porch-front homes at prices that allow full renovations. Success depends on recent renovated comparable sales nearby. Our Pre-Offer Rehab Review checks those sales to test whether your refinance target is realistic.

faqs.q: Can you prepare a Baltimore rental for its lead certificate?
faqs.a: Yes. We plan rehab scopes to meet Maryland's lead risk reduction standards for pre-1978 rentals, including window treatment or replacement, paint stabilization, lead-safe work practices and specialized cleaning before dust-wipe testing. We coordinate timing so the inspection can happen as soon as work is complete, which helps you obtain the certificate needed for city rental licensing and tenant move-in without paying for an extra week of vacancy.

faqs.q: Does Genstone offer loans for Baltimore BRRRR projects?
faqs.a: Genstone Financial, part of the Genstone Companies, provides fix-and-flip loans, DSCR rental loans, lines of credit and new construction loans. Investors often use rehab financing for purchase and construction, then refinance into a DSCR loan once the property is leased. You are welcome to use other lenders, and our scopes and draw records are organized to fit typical lender processes.

rental-renovation.title: Rental Property Renovation in Baltimore, MD | Genstone
rental-renovation.metaDescription: Baltimore single-family rental renovations and turns: one spec across rowhouse eras, lead certificates at turnover, licensing-ready units, remote tracking.
rental-renovation.intro: Every turnover in a pre-1978 Baltimore rental is also a lead compliance event. Maryland requires a new lead risk reduction certificate at each change of tenant, and the city's rental license depends on it. Add flat roofs, aging laterals, older boilers and the wear that comes with years of tenants, and a portfolio of Baltimore rows needs a steady, organized approach to renovation and turns. Genstone Construction renovates and turns single-family rentals across Baltimore and nearby Baltimore County for individual landlords, property managers, funds and REITs. We build a rental standard that fits the city's housing, coordinate vetted, licensed local contractors and assign a designated field manager to each property. Owners can review photos, milestones and draw status online, which makes it possible to manage scattered rows without visiting each one.

sections.h2: One standard for several generations of rowhouse
sections.body:
A Baltimore portfolio might include an alley house in Washington Hill, a formstone row in Highlandtown, a daylight row in Belair-Edison and a detached house in Lauraville. Four houses, four different weak points. We start with a rental standard that sets consistent finish choices across your properties: one flooring product, one paint palette, one cabinet line and one fixture package.

Then we adapt the standard to each house. An older alley house may need structural work on its stair, joists and rear wall, along with lead-safe window replacement. A formstone row may need facade repair, roof replacement and basement drainage. A daylight row may need porch framing, gutter repair and attention to its rear yard and alley access. A detached Lauraville home may need siding, foundation drainage and updated mechanicals. Writing each scope against a common standard makes it easier to compare costs across properties and plan capital improvements over several years, rather than reacting to one emergency at a time.

sections.h2: Turns built around Maryland lead compliance
sections.body:
In Baltimore, a rental turn for a pre-1978 unit is not complete until it can pass a lead inspection and dust-wipe testing for a new lead risk reduction certificate. That changes how a turn is planned. Our turn scopes include paint stabilization inside and out, window and friction-surface checks, repairs to damaged trim and doors, lead-safe work practices and specialized cleaning before testing.

We also cover the standard turn items: patching and painting, flooring repair or replacement, fixture and appliance checks, new smoke and carbon monoxide alarms and a review of handrails, egress and heat. A look at the roof, basement, sewer cleanout and back building can catch problems before they become emergencies. Genstone Field Services, part of the Genstone Companies, provides turn and make-ready work, inspections and occupied maintenance, so owners can use one team for renovation and ongoing care. Coordinating the lead inspection with the end of the turn reduces vacancy between tenants.

sections.h2: The systems behind Baltimore landlord calls
sections.body:
The most expensive calls for Baltimore landlords tend to involve water. Flat roofs leak at party walls and back building junctions. Clay and cast-iron laterals back up into basements during heavy rain. Galvanized supply lines leak inside walls. Older boilers fail in cold weather, and window air conditioners installed by tenants can damage sashes and trim.

Renovation is the right time to address those systems because walls and ceilings are already open. Our rental scopes often include roof replacement with proper flashing, a camera inspection and repair of the sewer lateral, a backwater valve, new supply lines, an updated electrical panel and either a serviced boiler or a new forced-air system with central air. Replacing original windows also helps with lead compliance and reduces drafts. These steps cost more upfront but cut emergency calls, insurance claims and vacancy, and the documentation we provide supports refinancing, sale or transitions between property managers.

faqs.q: Do you renovate rentals in Baltimore County?
faqs.a: Yes. Many Baltimore-area portfolios include homes in Dundalk, Essex, Parkville, Catonsville and other Baltimore County communities. Permits and rental requirements outside the city are handled by the county, and Maryland's lead law still applies to pre-1978 rentals. Your field manager confirms the rules for each address and plans the renovation and turn process accordingly. Formstone and daylight rows in Dundalk and Essex age much like their city counterparts, so the same rental standard usually carries over with small adjustments.

faqs.q: How do you handle lead compliance at turnover?
faqs.a: We plan each turn so the unit can pass the inspection and dust-wipe testing required for a new lead risk reduction certificate. That includes stabilizing paint, checking and treating windows and friction surfaces, repairing damaged trim, using lead-safe practices and performing specialized cleaning. We coordinate timing with the inspector so the certificate can be issued promptly and the unit can be leased.

faqs.q: Can I manage a Baltimore rental portfolio from out of state?
faqs.a: Yes. Each property has a designated field manager who posts photos, milestones and draw information online as work progresses. You can review scopes, approve change orders and track multiple properties remotely. Many of our Baltimore clients are out-of-state or institutional owners who rely on documentation rather than site visits to manage renovations and turns. Lead certificates, license inspection reports and permit records are stored with each property's file.

multifamily-renovation.title: Duplex and 2-4 Unit Renovation, Baltimore MD | Genstone
multifamily-renovation.metaDescription: Renovating Baltimore 2-4 unit rowhouses in Reservoir Hill, Charles Village and Bolton Hill: legal unit counts, BMZA approvals, fire separation, CHAP review.
multifamily-renovation.h1: Duplex and 2–4 Unit Renovations in Baltimore
multifamily-renovation.intro: Baltimore's small multifamily stock lives inside its grandest rowhouses. Three- and four-story Victorian rows in Reservoir Hill, Bolton Hill, Mount Vernon and Charles Village were divided into apartments decades ago, often one per floor, and some larger porch-front houses in other neighborhoods were split into two units. Many conversions predate current rules, and some were never approved at all. Genstone Construction renovates two- to four-unit properties in Baltimore for investors, funds and lenders. Our free Pre-Offer Rehab Review estimates the work and helps you confirm the legal unit count before closing, since that count drives value, financing and licensing. After closing, a designated field manager coordinates vetted, licensed local contractors, permits through Housing and Community Development, CHAP review where needed and phasing around tenants, with each unit tracked separately.

sections.h2: Legal units and zoning approvals in Baltimore
sections.body:
Under Baltimore's zoning code, converting a rowhouse into multiple units, or adding a unit to an existing conversion, generally requires zoning approval and often a hearing before the Board of Municipal and Zoning Appeals. Many buildings have more apartments than the city recognizes, and each unlicensed unit is a problem for financing, insurance and rental licensing.

Before buying, we recommend confirming the building's legal use and unit count through city records. If the current layout exceeds what is approved, you can value the building at its legal count or plan to seek approval, understanding that the outcome is not certain. We put a number on each route. Legalizing a unit typically requires fire-rated separation between units, rated doors, interconnected alarms, code-compliant egress, separate utilities and a full kitchen and bath. Removing an extra unit may be simpler and still produce a strong rental. Knowing the cost of each path before closing protects you from paying for income the building cannot legally produce.

sections.h2: Shared systems, egress and historic review
sections.body:
Older Baltimore conversions often share one boiler, one water heater and a single electric service split into subpanels. Upper-floor units may rely on a single interior stair, and separation between floors may be original plaster and lath. In tall Victorian rows, egress from third- and fourth-floor units is a major safety and code concern.

Our scopes separate what the code requires for the building's legal use from what makes economic sense. Fire separation, rated doors, interconnected smoke and carbon monoxide alarms and safe egress are requirements. Separate electric meters and panels let tenants pay for their own power. Individual HVAC systems, often ductless units in rows without ductwork, simplify billing and comfort. In CHAP districts such as Bolton Hill, Mount Vernon and Union Square, exterior changes like new rear stairs, doors or windows require approval, so we plan designs that meet safety needs while respecting preservation rules and allow time for review.

Many small multifamily buildings in Baltimore are bought with tenants in place. Rent from occupied units can offset holding costs while vacant units are renovated. We phase work so occupied apartments keep heat, water and safe access. Shared-system work, such as roof replacement, electrical service upgrades, boiler replacement or sewer lateral repair, is scheduled with advance notice and kept short.

Lead safety is especially important in occupied pre-1978 buildings. Each rental unit needs its own lead risk reduction certificate, and dust from work in one unit can travel through shared stairs and halls. We contain work areas, clean daily and coordinate access with tenants. As vacant units are completed and certified, we move to the next as it turns over. Your field manager tracks scope, progress and costs for each unit and posts photos and milestone updates, so the draw record matches the work completed in each apartment and supports licensing, refinancing or sale.

faqs.q: Can you add a unit to a Baltimore rowhouse?
faqs.a: Sometimes. Adding a unit generally requires zoning approval and often a hearing before the Board of Municipal and Zoning Appeals. If approval is granted, construction typically includes fire separation, egress, separate utilities and kitchen and bathroom work. We can estimate construction costs so you can weigh them against the approval process, the timeline and the additional rent the unit would produce.

faqs.q: Do CHAP historic districts affect multifamily renovations?
faqs.a: Yes, for exterior work. Buildings in CHAP districts such as Bolton Hill, Mount Vernon, Union Square and Butchers Hill need approval for exterior changes like windows, doors, rear stairs and masonry. Interior renovations follow standard permitting through Housing and Community Development. We plan exterior items around the review process and start interior work while approvals are pending, so the building keeps moving toward occupancy.

faqs.q: Does each apartment need its own lead certificate?
faqs.a: Yes, for pre-1978 rental units under Maryland's lead law. Each unit must be registered with the Maryland Department of the Environment and obtain a lead risk reduction certificate, including at turnover. Our scopes plan lead-safe work, window treatment and specialized cleaning for each unit so they can pass inspection and dust testing and move toward licensing without delay. Scheduling unit inspections together, where vacancies allow, can also save time.

fha-203k.title: FHA 203(k) Contractor in Baltimore, MD | Genstone
fha-203k.metaDescription: FHA 203(k) certified contractor in Baltimore: bids for daylight rows and Hamilton bungalows, Limited vs Standard guidance, VBN checks and lender draws.
fha-203k.intro: A daylight row in Ednor Gardens-Lakeside or a bungalow in Hamilton can be a first-time buyer's best path into a Baltimore neighborhood, if the repairs can be financed. The FHA 203(k) program makes that possible by combining the purchase and renovation into one loan. Genstone Construction holds FHA 203(k) Certified Contractor status, and we prepare the itemized bids, scopes and draw schedules lenders and HUD consultants need. We work with buyers, agents and loan officers to sort out whether a property fits the Limited or Standard program and to flag Baltimore-specific issues, such as Vacant Building Notices, failing back buildings and porch framing, that affect eligibility and budget. During construction, a designated field manager coordinates vetted local contractors, permits through Housing and Community Development and the lender's draw process.

sections.h2: Limited or Standard for a Baltimore home
sections.body:
Limited 203(k) loans fund up to $75,000 of non-structural work. For many daylight rows and northeast bungalows, that can cover a new flat roof membrane, replacement windows, kitchen and bath updates, a new furnace or boiler, central air, electrical panel replacement, plumbing updates, flooring and paint. Structural work such as rebuilding a rear wall, underpinning a back building or replacing joists falls outside the Limited program.

The Standard 203(k) is designed for heavier projects. It requires at least $5,000 in repairs and a HUD-approved 203(k) consultant who prepares a work write-up and oversees draws. In Baltimore, Standard loans are common for older rows where back buildings have separated, joists have rotted at the party walls or porches need structural rebuilding. Standard loans take longer to close, so identifying the right program early is important. We help agents and buyers see quickly which program a house likely needs, keeping the transaction on a realistic schedule.

sections.h2: Which Baltimore houses fit the 203(k) program
sections.body:
Daylight rows in Belair-Edison, Ednor Gardens-Lakeside, Waverly and Edmondson Village are strong 203(k) candidates. They tend to have solid brick construction, porches and usable basements, with dated kitchens, baths and mechanicals that a renovation can modernize. Detached homes and bungalows in Hamilton and Lauraville often fit the Limited program when systems and finishes need work but the structure is sound.

Older rows in Highlandtown, Pigtown or Charles Village can work too, but deserve careful inspection, since rear walls, joists and roofs may push a project into the Standard program. Properties with Vacant Building Notices can be financed, but the scope must include work to clear the notice before occupancy. Because nearly all Baltimore houses predate 1978, FHA lead-based paint requirements apply when painted surfaces are disturbed, and our scopes include lead-safe work. Agents who send listings early allow us to flag structural issues and VBN status before the buyer makes an offer.

sections.h2: Bids, consultants and draws in Baltimore
sections.body:
Every Baltimore 203(k) bid we write itemizes repairs with labor and materials, lists the permits Housing and Community Development will require and proposes a draw schedule tied to completed milestones. On Standard loans, our numbers are reconciled with the consultant's write-up; on Limited loans, the bid follows the lender's required format.

From the day the loan closes, your field manager runs the local trades and sends regular updates to the buyer, agent, lender and consultant. Each draw follows the lender's inspection and approval process, and the program's $15,000 threshold can bring additional inspections on larger projects. Lien waivers accompany each payment. Many buyers are paying rent until they move in, so we prioritize heat, electrical, plumbing and the roof to make the home livable early. If the property had a VBN, your field manager coordinates the inspections needed to clear it. At completion, the buyer receives project records and our one-year workmanship warranty, which covers our installation but not wear or damage after move-in.

faqs.q: Can a 203(k) loan buy a Baltimore house with a VBN?
faqs.a: It can, as long as the renovation scope corrects the violations and the city clears the notice before the buyer occupies the home. That usually means permitted work and inspections through Housing and Community Development. Depending on the repairs needed, the project may require a Standard 203(k). We review VBN status during the bid process so the scope and timeline reflect it.

faqs.q: Can a 203(k) loan add central air to a Baltimore row?
faqs.a: Yes. Installing central air or ductless systems is generally an eligible improvement under both Limited and Standard 203(k) loans, as long as the overall scope fits program rules. In rows heated by radiators, ductless systems or small-duct high-velocity systems are often practical. We price options during the bid so the buyer can choose the approach that fits the house and budget.

faqs.q: Do you work with Baltimore agents on 203(k) purchases?
faqs.a: Yes. Agents often send us listings or inspection reports so we can estimate repairs, identify the likely program and deliver a bid quickly. Our free Pre-Offer Rehab Review is available to buyers and agents, not only investors. We stay in contact with the loan officer and consultant through closing and construction, which lets the agent focus on the transaction rather than contractor coordination.

reo-renovation.title: REO Property Renovation in Baltimore, MD | Genstone
reo-renovation.metaDescription: REO and bank-owned renovation in Baltimore: Vacant Building Notices, frozen boilers, roof and rear-wall failures, ground rent checks and line-item reporting.
reo-renovation.h1: REO and Bank-Owned Renovations in Baltimore
reo-renovation.intro: Bank-owned rowhouses in Baltimore often arrive with layered problems. The house may carry a Vacant Building Notice, open code violations or a ground rent that complicates title. Inside, a boiler may have frozen and cracked, a flat roof may have been leaking for months, scrappers may have taken copper, and the back building may be pulling away from the main house. Mortgage servicers, banks, REITs, investment funds and other lenders send us these assets, and Government-Sponsored Enterprises count Genstone among their preferred contractors. We coordinate vetted, licensed local contractors in Baltimore and the surrounding counties to secure, repair and prepare REO properties for sale or rent. Each asset receives a designated field manager, a line-item scope and photo documentation, so asset managers can approve work and report on it without traveling to Maryland. Genstone Field Services also provides preservation, inspections and code compliance.

sections.h2: Vacant Building Notices and city compliance
sections.body:
Baltimore's Department of Housing and Community Development issues Vacant Building Notices on properties it considers vacant and unfit, and many REO assets carry one by the time a servicer takes title. A VBN generally means the house cannot be legally occupied until violations are corrected under permit and the city clears the notice. Open code violations for debris, overgrowth, open openings or unsafe conditions can add fines and liability.

Our REO work in Baltimore often starts with compliance. We review VBN status and open notices, secure the property, remove debris and scope corrective work. When the disposition plan calls for occupancy, we identify every repair needed to clear the VBN, including structural, roof and system work, and pull the necessary permits. Photo documentation of each correction helps your team respond to city notices and maintain a clean record. For properties that will be sold as-is to investors, documenting VBN status and condition clearly helps buyers price the asset accurately and reduces post-closing disputes.

sections.h2: Freeze, roof and structural damage in vacant rows
sections.body:
Vacant Baltimore rows deteriorate in predictable ways. Boilers and radiators freeze and crack without proper winterization, and burst supply lines flood floors and ceilings. Flat roofs leak at party walls and back building junctions, and without anyone noticing, water rots joists, ceilings and stairs. Rear walls and back buildings can separate from the main house. Scrappers strip copper pipe, wiring and fixtures, and open houses can attract squatters and vandalism.

Our REO scopes begin with a careful inspection of the roof, rear wall, back building foundation, heating system, plumbing and electrical. Typical items include roof replacement with proper flashing, structural repairs to joists and rear walls, pressure testing supply lines, replacing frozen boilers or radiators, removing water-damaged plaster and treating mold. Stolen copper and wiring are scoped for full replacement. Each condition is documented with photos and itemized so asset managers can file claims, approve repairs and decide on disposition with accurate information.

sections.h2: Title, ground rent and the repair path
sections.body:
Some Baltimore properties are subject to ground rent, a Maryland arrangement in which the land is leased separately from the house. Ground rents and municipal liens can complicate title and sale. Genstone Title Clearing & Escrow, part of the Genstone Companies, works on title issues, and our field documentation helps keep the repair side moving while those questions are resolved.

On the repair side, not every Baltimore REO needs the same treatment. Some sell best to investors after securing and cleanup, particularly where VBNs and structural issues are severe. Others sell faster and for more after targeted repairs that clear the VBN and make the house financeable for owner-occupants. In neighborhoods with strong renovated sales, a fuller renovation can make sense. We can prepare multiple scopes for an asset, each with cost and projected value. Labor, materials and debris removal are itemized, lien waivers and contractor compliance records are collected, and invoices follow your approval process, providing a clear record for investors, GSE partners and auditors.

faqs.q: Can you clear a Vacant Building Notice on an REO property?
faqs.a: We can scope and complete the permitted work needed to correct the violations behind a VBN and coordinate the inspections required for the city to clear it. The scope depends on the property's condition and may include structural, roof, electrical, plumbing and safety work. We document each correction with photos so your team has a complete record for the city and for buyers.

faqs.q: Do you secure and winterize Baltimore REO properties?
faqs.a: Yes. Securing, winterizing, debris removal and inspections all fall to Genstone Field Services, our preservation company. In Baltimore, proper winterization is critical because many rows rely on boilers and radiators that freeze and crack, and securing helps reduce scrapping and squatting. When a disposition plan is set, Genstone Construction can carry the property into renovation using the same intake records, so condition photos from day one remain part of the asset file.

faqs.q: What reporting do you provide on Baltimore REO assets?
faqs.a: Each Baltimore asset receives an itemized estimate, before and after photos for every scope line, milestone updates and a file of permits, inspections, VBN status, lien waivers and contractor compliance records. Reporting can be adapted to your platform or approval workflow, allowing asset managers, servicers and GSE partners to review and audit work without visiting the property. Ground rent or title questions flagged during intake are noted in the same file.
